query: For phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys, what single intervention could improve glass-forming ability and the thermal stability of the amorphous state? Formulate one testable hypothesis that specifies the intervention without presupposing its class, the mechanism by which it would act, the predicted improvement relative to an otherwise comparable baseline, the conditions under which it should or should not work, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled isothermal annealing treatment applied to as-quenched, phosphorus-containing high‐entropy alloys will trigger a glass-to‐glass transition that produces a structurally relaxed, low‐energy amorphous state. This state exhibits a higher onset temperature for crystallization (i.e. improved thermal stability) while maintaining an excellent glass-forming ability.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-quenched, fully amorphous phosphorus-containing high‐entropy alloy (e.g. Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20) produced by rapid cooling.
generation.intervention: Apply a single controlled isothermal annealing treatment at a temperature slightly below the crystallization onset (around Tg – 5 K) for a fixed period (e.g. 1–2 hours) in an inert atmosphere.
generation.conditions: The treatment must be performed under well-controlled thermal conditions such that the annealing temperature is sufficiently high to enable atomic rearrangement (relaxation) but remains below the threshold for nucleation of crystalline phases; afterward, rapid cooling is required to freeze in the relaxed structure.
generation.structural_mediator: Local structural relaxation and reduction in free volume, particularly in phosphorus-rich regions, that facilitates atomic reorganization into a denser, lower-energy amorphous configuration.
generation.mechanism: The annealing encourages a glass-to‐glass transition via thermally activated atomic rearrangements without triggering crystallization. This results in a more stable amorphous matrix with a higher energy barrier for subsequent crystallization, thereby enhancing thermal stability while preserving the amorphous (glass-forming) state.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated as-quenched state, the annealed alloy will exhibit a higher crystallization onset temperature in DSC measurements and greater resistance to crystallization upon reheating, while still displaying the amorphous diffraction signature in XRD/TEM.
generation.baseline: The untreated, rapidly solidified amorphous phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy.
generation.boundary: If the annealing temperature is too close to the crystallization temperature or the time is too long, partial crystallization may occur, negating the benefits. Similarly, annealing at too low a temperature may not induce the necessary relaxation, so the beneficial effects are bounded to a narrow annealing temperature–time window.
generation.uncertainty: This proposal combines findings from the studies demonstrating phosphorus’s role in promoting amorphization and modifying crystallization pathways (e.g. PMC11642357::web::020::4_discussion) with reports of glass‐to‐glass transitions in high‐entropy metallic glasses (e.g. PMC9023469::web::019::4_discussion). While similar thermal treatments have been shown to relax the amorphous state in other systems, the optimal annealing parameters and detailed atomic-scale rearrangements in phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys remain untested and require further elucidation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a batch of as-quenched, amorphous Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy samples. Divide the batch into two groups. Group A undergoes a controlled isothermal annealing treatment at Tg – 5 K (determined via preliminary DSC) for 2 hours under an inert atmosphere followed by rapid quenching. Group B serves as the control (no annealing). Compare both groups using DSC to measure crystallization onset temperatures, XRD/TEM to confirm the amorphous structure, and cyclic thermal stability tests to assess resistance to crystallization.
measurements: DSC for crystallization onset temperature and heat flow exotherms
XRD and TEM for phase identification (amorphous vs crystalline)
Thermal cycling tests to assess reproducibility of the thermal stability
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples (Group A) show no significant increase in the crystallization onset temperature, or if they develop detectable crystalline phases compared to the control Group B, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Furthermore, recent findings on NiNbP bulk metallic glasses highlight how phosphorus additions enhance glass-forming ability and increase hardness, albeit at the cost of some ductility []. Inspired by these results, this study explores the microstructure, mechanical behavior, and phase stability of phosphorus-containing alloys to better understand and utilize their unique properties. The combination of high configurational entropy and phosphorus enrichment in these alloys suggests their potential for applications in demanding environments that require enhanced wear resistance, corrosion resistance, and thermal stability. These properties position them as promising candidates for use in the aerospace, automotive, and tooling industries, as well as in advanced coating technologies and high-performance structural components. Previous studies reported its melting temperatures as 1607 K [,], 1523 K [], and 1543 K [], indicating a relatively narrow range of solidification. In contrast, the Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 alloy containing phosphorus exhibits a significantly broader solidification temperature range and more complex crystallization behavior. Pronounced thermal effects were observed at T3 = 1291 K and T4 = 1206 K during slow cooling on a copper plate (52 K/s), and at T3 = 977 K and T4 = 960 K during rapid cooling following a brief electric arc pulse (3018 K/s). This marked reduction in solidification temperatures compared to the Cantor alloy demonstrates the role of phosphorus in modifying thermal behavior and promoting amorphization. These results highlight the critical importance of controlling cooling rates and alloy composition to optimize phase stability and microstructure.
